title: Pulling a whole table out of a page

blocks.text:
# Week 8, Day 3.1 — TypeScript for reading a table

Four concepts. Today you pull a whole table out of a page and turn it into data you can check.

> **Every run starts fresh.** Each time you press Run, your code starts from a clean slate. Nothing from a previous run is still in memory.

| # | Concept | Why today needs it |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | The classic `for` loop | Walk rows by index, and rows inside rows. |
| 2 | Arrays of arrays | A table *is* rows of cells. |
| 3 | `.map()` and `.push()` | Turn elements into values. |
| 4 | Typed functions | Make the scrape reusable instead of a one-off. |

Already covered — links only: arrays and `forEach` in [Day 2.1](/learn/w8/d2/p1); `async`/`await`,
template literals and destructuring in [Day 1.1](/learn/w8/d1/p1).

## 1. The classic `for` loop, and loops inside loops

`forEach` walks a list. A `for` loop does the same but exposes the counter, which you need when
one loop sits inside another.

A table needs two: the outer walks **rows**, the inner walks that row's **cells**.

**Expected:**

```
row 0: [0]Smith [1]John [2]$50.00
row 1: [0]Bach [1]Frank [2]$51.00
```

`i` is the row, `j` is the cell. Reusing `i` in both loops is the classic bug — the inner loop
overwrites the outer counter and you get an infinite loop or skipped rows.

**Challenge:** print only the second column.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

## 2. Arrays of arrays

`string[][]` reads as "an array of arrays of strings" — a table. `table[1][2]` is row 1, cell 2,
both counting from zero.

**Expected:** `2`, `3`, `$51.00`, the JSON, then `[ "Smith", "Bach" ]`.

That last line is the shape you want most often: one column, pulled out for checking.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

## 3. `.map()` and `.push()`

- **`.map()`** — turn every item into something else, giving a **new** array of the same length.
- **`.push()`** — add one item to the end of an existing array.

Both build the same result; `.map()` is shorter when there's one value per input.

**Expected:** `[ 50, 51, 100 ]` twice, then `total: 201`.

`Number("$50.00")` is `NaN` — the `$` has to go first. Scraped text is *always* strings, so
converting is part of the job.

**Challenge:** make a `string[][]` of two rows and use `.map()` to get just the last cell of each.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

## 4. Typed functions — the difference between a snippet and a tool

A function with a parameter can be reused. Hardcode the table name inside and you'll paste a
second copy for the second table.

```ts
async function scrapeTable(page: Page, tableSelector: string): Promise<string[][]>
```

Read it as: takes a page and a selector, hands back a table of strings, and does so
asynchronously.

**Expected:** three arrays — one per column.

One function, three answers. Had `index` been hardcoded you'd have written `columnOfLastNames`,
`columnOfFirstNames`, `columnOfDues` — which is exactly the duplication Day 2.2 warned about,
in a different costume.

## Recap

| Concept | Remember |
|---|---|
| Nested `for` | Outer = rows, inner = cells. Never reuse the counter. |
| `string[][]` | `table[row][cell]`, both from 0. |
| `.map()` / `.push()` | Scraped text is always a string — convert it. |
| Typed functions | A parameter is what makes it reusable. |

**Next:** [Day 3.2 — Scraping a real page](/learn/w8/d3/p2)

blocks.text:
# Week 8, Day 3.2 — Pulling a whole table out of a page

By the end you will have read every row of a live web table into an array and checked it —
using one function that works on any table you point it at.

> **Try it here.** Write code in the editor on the right and press Run. Your code drives a real browser, and the results appear beside it.

Target page: [https://the-internet.herokuapp.com/tables](https://the-internet.herokuapp.com/tables) — two tables holding the same data with different markup.

## What scraping is, and when you actually need it

Scraping means reading a page's content as *data* rather than checking one value at a time.
It's also called crawling when it walks between pages.

It is huge in data and AI work — Python's `pandas` can read an HTML table in one line — and
comparatively rare in testing, because a test usually has one focused expectation, not a
thousand rows.

But it earns its place when the expectation *is* the whole set:

| Situation | Why one-at-a-time fails |
|---|---|
| "All 10 orders I created appear" | 10 separate assertions, and no check that there aren't 11 |
| "This column is sorted" | Sorting is a property of the list, not of any row |
| "The total equals the sum of rows" | You need every row to add them up |

Playwright gives you about 95% of what testing needs as ready-made API. Scraping is in the
other 5% — it's plain JavaScript running in the page, and you write the logic yourself.

## `$` and `$$`, `$eval` and `$$eval`

Four names, one idea:

| Call | Returns | Think of it as |
|---|---|---|
| `page.$(sel)` | the **first** match, or `null` | `querySelector` |
| `page.$$(sel)` | **all** matches, as an array | `querySelectorAll` |
| `page.$eval(sel, fn)` | runs `fn` on the first match, **in the browser**, returns the result |
| `page.$$eval(sel, fn)` | runs `fn` on **all** matches, in the browser |

The `eval` pair is what makes scraping fast: the loop runs *inside the page* and only the
finished data crosses back. Pulling 4 rows × 6 cells across one at a time would be 24 round trips.

One dollar = one element. Two dollars = all of them.

**Coming from Selenium?** `$` is `findElement`, `$$` is `findElements` — the same one-versus-many
split you already know, with shorter names. The `eval` pair has no direct Selenium equivalent;
the nearest thing is `JavascriptExecutor`.

## Example 1 — look before you scrape

**Objective:** confirm the structure before writing a selector. Guessing is how scrapes break.

**Expected:** both tables report 6 headers (`Last Name`, `First Name`, `Email`, `Due`,
`Web Site`, `Action`), 4 body rows, 6 cells per row.

Two things this told us, and both matter:

- **`tbody` is doing real work.** Without it you'd also match the header row and get 5 rows,
  then wonder why row 0 says "Last Name".
- **Both tables hold the same data.** So a function written for one should work on the other
  unchanged — which is the test we'll run in Example 3.

**Challenge:** count `#table1 tr` without `tbody`. What number comes back, and why?

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

## Example 2 — read every row

**Objective:** get the table into a `string[][]`.

**Expected:**

```
rows: 4
  ["Smith","John","jsmith@gmail.com","$50.00","http://www.jsmith.com","edit delete"]
  ["Bach","Frank","fbach@yahoo.com","$51.00","http://www.frank.com","edit delete"]
  ["Doe","Jason","jdoe@hotmail.com","$100.00","http://www.jdoe.com","edit delete"]
  ["Conway","Tim","tconway@earthlink.net","$50.00","http://www.timconway.com","edit delete"]
```

…followed by the same data as a grid, from `console.table(rows)`. Worth remembering while
exploring — a 4×6 grid is far easier to eyeball than four JSON strings.

Line by line:

| Piece | What it does |
|---|---|
| `$$eval("#table1 tbody tr", fn)` | finds every body row, runs `fn` **inside the browser** |
| `trs.map(tr => …)` | one output row per table row |
| `tr.querySelectorAll("td")` | that row's cells — plain DOM, because we're in the page now |
| `Array.from(…)` | `querySelectorAll` returns a NodeList, not an array; `.map` needs an array |
| `.replace(/\s+/g, " ").trim()` | collapse the newlines HTML leaves in `edit\n delete` |

That last one is not cosmetic. Without it the final cell is `"edit\n            delete"` and
every comparison against `"edit delete"` fails.

**Challenge:** drop the `.replace(...)` and print the last cell with `JSON.stringify` to see the
raw whitespace.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

## Example 3 — make it a tool

**Objective:** the same function, on both tables, unchanged.

Example 2 hardcodes `#table1`. Move that to a parameter and it works anywhere.

**Expected:** `4`, `4`, `identical data: true`.

Different markup, same values — so the function reads *content*, not layout. That is the
difference between a scrape that survives a redesign and one that doesn't.

**Challenge:** call it with `#table3`. What comes back — an error, or an empty array? Knowing
which decides whether your code needs a guard.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

## Example 4 — now check something you couldn't check row by row

**Objective:** use the scraped table to assert a property of the *whole* list.

**Expected:**

```
dues: [ 50, 51, 100, 50 ]
sorted copy: [ 50, 50, 51, 100 ]
is the column sorted? false
total due: 251
```

`[...dues]` copies before sorting, because `.sort()` **rearranges the original**. Sort `dues`
directly and you've destroyed the evidence you were about to compare against — a genuinely
nasty bug, because the comparison then always passes.

None of these three checks — sorted, total, full column — can be written as a per-row
assertion. That's when scraping is the right tool.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

## The modern alternative: locators

`$$eval` takes one snapshot, immediately. If the table is still loading you scrape an empty page.

Locators re-query and auto-wait:

**Expected:** `4`, the first row's six cells, then the four email addresses.

| | `$$eval` | Locator |
|---|---|---|
| Waiting | none — snapshot now | auto-waits |
| Best for | complex per-row logic in one trip | counts, text, assertions |
| Reads as | JavaScript in the page | Playwright |

**Rule of thumb:** if a CSS selector alone gets you there, use a locator. Reach for `$$eval` when
you need real logic per row — walking cells, building objects, computing as you go.

Both are correct. Knowing why you picked one is the part that matters.
## The same scrape, as a real spec

> ▶ **Run it yourself:** `npx playwright test week8/generated/day3-scrape-tables.spec.ts`

**Expected:** `5 passed`.

## Best practices

- **Inspect first**, then write the selector. `tbody` or not is a real decision.
- **Normalise whitespace** — HTML is full of newlines you didn't ask for.
- **Convert types explicitly.** Everything scraped is a string.
- **Copy before sorting** (`[...arr].sort()`).
- **Pass the selector in.** A hardcoded one guarantees a second copy of the function.
- **Prefer locators** unless you need per-row logic.

## Common mistakes

| You see | Usually means | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Row 0 is the header text | selector missed `tbody` | `#table1 tbody tr` |
| `"edit\n     delete"` | raw HTML whitespace | `.replace(/\s+/g, " ").trim()` |
| `NaN` in a total | forgot to strip `$` | `Number(t.replace("$", ""))` |
| "Sorted" always passes | sorted the array in place | `[...arr].sort()` |
| Empty array, no error | selector matched nothing | check `count()` first |
| `.map is not a function` | `querySelectorAll` gives a NodeList | wrap in `Array.from(...)` |

**Next:** [Day 3.3](/learn/w8/d3/p3) — making this a component a whole suite can use.

parts.title: A table reader the whole suite can use

blocks.text:
# Week 8, Day 3.3 — A table reader the whole suite can use

Same `$$eval` call as [Day 3.2](/learn/w8/d3/p2). No new API. What changes is the **shape of what
comes back**, and where the function lives.

## The problem with `string[][]`

`scrapeTable` works. But look at what a test using it has to say:

```ts
const dues = table.map((row) => Number(row[3].replace("$", "")));
```

`row[3]` is the Due column — today. Insert a column and every test silently reads the wrong one.
Nothing fails; the numbers are just wrong, which is worse than a crash.

| Returning | A test has to say | Breaks when |
|---|---|---|
| `string[][]` | `row[3]` | a column moves |
| `Record<string, string>[]` | `row.Due` | the *header text* changes — visible, and it fails loudly |

Keying by header is the same instinct as a page object: refer to things by what they mean, not
where they sit.

Now a test reads like a sentence:

```ts
const rows = await readTable(page, "#table1");
expect(rows[0]["First Name"]).toBe("John");
expect(rows.map((r) => r.Email)).toContain("jsmith@gmail.com");
```

| Choice | Reason |
|---|---|
| Headers read via locator, rows via `$$eval` | headers are 6 strings (locator is clearer); rows need per-cell logic (one round trip) |
| `Record<string, string>` | keyed by meaning, not position |
| `cells[i] ?? ""` | a short row yields `""`, not `undefined` sneaking into a comparison |
| Whitespace normalised in both | otherwise `"Due "` and `"Due"` are different keys — a maddening bug |
| No `expect()` anywhere | same rule as Day 1.3's API client |

## Where it belongs

This is not a page object — it isn't tied to one screen. It's a **component**: a reusable piece
of behaviour that any page object or test can call.

```
framework/
├── pages/          one class per screen
├── components/     reusable widgets — a table reader lives here
└── fixtures.ts
```

Once it's a component, a page object can expose meaning instead of mechanics:

```ts
class OrdersPage {
  async orders(): Promise<Record<string, string>[]> {
    return readTable(this.page, "#orders");
  }
}
```

The test then says `await ordersPage.orders()` and never learns that a table was involved. If the
orders list becomes a grid of cards tomorrow, one method changes and every test still passes.

> The repo has no `framework/` folder yet — it was removed in the August 2026 reset. This is the
> shape being demonstrated, not a file you can import. Later weeks build the real thing.

## When *not* to reach for this

Scraping is genuinely rare in testing, and reaching for it by default produces slow, brittle
tests that assert far more than they mean to.

| Use a plain assertion | Use a table reader |
|---|---|
| "This one row exists" | "These 10 rows exist and no others" |
| "The status says Shipped" | "Every row's status is Shipped" |
| "The total shows £251" | "The total equals the sum of the rows" |

The honest summary: `expect(page.getByRole("row")).toHaveCount(4)` beats a scrape whenever it
answers the question, because it auto-waits and fails with a clear message. Scrape when the
expectation genuinely spans the whole set.

## What a reviewer checks

- **No assertions inside the reader** — it returns data; the test judges it.
- **No column indexes in tests** — key by header.
- **Whitespace normalised**, headers and cells alike.
- **`count()` checked** before trusting an empty result.
- **A locator would not have done the job** more simply.

**Next:** [Day 3.4](/learn/w8/d3/p4) — your turn.

# Week 8, Day 3.4 — Practice

Three problems. No answer key.

Target page: [https://the-internet.herokuapp.com/tables](https://the-internet.herokuapp.com/tables) — `#table1` and `#table2`, same data, different markup.

> Stuck past twenty minutes? Back to [Day 3.1](/learn/w8/d3/p1) or [Day 3.2](/learn/w8/d3/p2).

## When you're done

**For each of your three answers, could a plain locator assertion have done it?**
For Problem 1's row count — yes, and `toHaveCount(4)` would have been better: it auto-waits and
fails more clearly. For "the totals add up" — no.

Knowing which tool is *unnecessary* is worth as much as knowing how to use it. Scraping is
powerful and slow; reach for it when the expectation spans the whole set, not because it feels
thorough.

## One principle to carry out of the week

"Can this be automated?" nearly always reduces to one question: **can you identify the element
reliably?** If you can address it, you can drive it. If you can't, no tool rescues you — and
that is why a stable locator matters more than any clever technique.

It comes up in interviews as *"name something that can't be automated"*, where the stock
answers are captchas and OTPs. The honest answer is that they *can* be — they're deliberately
built to resist automation, not impossible. In practice you have them disabled or stubbed in
test environments, because a test that defeats your own captcha is also proof the captcha
doesn't work.

If a locator won't hold, don't reach for a hand-written XPath. Ask Playwright: `npx playwright
codegen <url>` records a page and suggests locators, and its suggestions favour role, label and
placeholder — the things least likely to change in a redesign. Fragile locators are the single
largest source of flaky UI suites, and this is the cheapest defence.

## Where this week landed

| Day | Built |
|---|---|
| [Day 1](/learn/w8/d1/p1) | tokens, headers, full CRUD against a live API |
| [Day 2](/learn/w8/d2/p1) | negative scenarios, four real defects, data-driven tests |
| Day 3 | reading a page as data, and when not to |

Three things decide whether automation works, in this order: **how well you know the
application**, then the tool, then the language. Playwright hands you roughly 95% ready-made —
today's `$$eval` loop was the other 5%, and it was plain JavaScript, not Playwright at all.

problems.statement:
**Build.** Scrape `#table1` and answer three questions with code:

1. How many rows are there?
2. What are all four email addresses?
3. What is the sum of the Due column?

**Check yourself.** The total is a number, not `NaN`. If you get `NaN`, you forgot the `$`.

> **Hint** — print one row with `JSON.stringify` before writing any index. Guessing which
> column is Due wastes more time than looking.

**Build.** A spec proving the two tables really hold the same data.

The page shows the same records twice with different markup — exactly the situation where a
scrape earns its keep.

1. Read both tables into keyed rows (`Record<string, string>[]`)
2. Assert they have the same number of rows
3. Assert every row matches, field by field, **without** relying on column position
4. Assert the Due column is **not** sorted — because it isn't, and a test that claims otherwise
   is a test that never ran

**Where.** A spec in `week8/generated/`.

**Check yourself.** Break it deliberately: change one expected email to something wrong and
confirm the failure message tells you *which row and which field*. If it just says
"expected false to be true", your assertions are too coarse to debug.

> **Hint** — comparing two arrays of objects with `toEqual` gives a much better diff than
> comparing two JSON strings.

**Build.** A reusable `TableReader` component, then use it for something a locator can't do.

1. A class or module taking a `Page` and a table selector
2. Methods: `rows()` returning keyed rows, `column(name)` returning one column by **header
   text**, and `count()`
3. A test that sorts the table by clicking a header, then proves the *scraped* order actually
   changed

**Where.** A spec in `week8/generated/`.

**Constraints — these are the exercise:**

- **No `expect()` inside the component**
- **No column indexes in the test** — header names only
- `column("Due")` must return numbers, not `"$50.00"` strings — decide where that conversion
  belongs and be able to defend it
- The test must pass **run on its own**

**Check yourself.** Run three times — passes every time. Then: could you point it at a table on
a different site without editing the class? If not, something is still hardcoded.

> **Hint** — the conversion question is the real design decision. A component that guesses which
> columns are numbers will guess wrong. What could the caller supply instead?
